clue.text: 27 finish with blunder in English type

parts.note: the last three letters of the answer to 27 spell a word for a lavatory, and john is a slang word for a lavatory
a bull is a ludicrous blunder in speech, as in an Irish bull

explanation.surface: Ending with a mistake in English print.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 ends in LOO, and john is another word for a lavatory. John Bull is the figure who personifies England.
explanation.definitionFit: The stout farmer figure is the traditional personification of the typical Englishman.

clue.text: See 1
Inclination to reverse Yorkshire river with bacterial infection

parts.note: a list is a ship's lean or tilt

indicators.note: to reverse means the river's name is read backwards

parts.note: the Aire is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A slope turning back a northern river, with a germ problem added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reverse' reads the river's name backwards. The Aire flows through Leeds; 'Inclination' here is a ship's tilt, not a preference.
explanation.definitionFit: Listeria is a bacterium causing listeriosis, a food-borne infection, and the name covers the illness loosely.

clue.text: Princess reportedly a duck

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so a word that sounds like the princess's name

parts.note: Princess Ida is the heroine of a Gilbert and Sullivan opera

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a royal lady is a waterbird.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British accent without a sounded R, IDA and EIDER sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck, famous for its soft down.

clue.text: Line I had otherwise abandoned, being intolerant of laxity

indicators.note: abandoned means those letters are dropped from the line's name

parts.note: the District line is a London Underground line

indicators.note: otherwise means the other way round, so the contraction is turned back to front

parts.note: I had contracts to I'D

explanation.surface: Someone strict has walked away from a line of thought they once held.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' turns ID (I'd) into DI, and 'abandoned' takes those letters off the front of DISTRICT, a London Underground line, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone strict is severe and does not tolerate lax behaviour, an adjectival phrase matching the adjective.

clue.text: Breaking into rubbish fifty-three times

indicators.note: breaking into means one piece forces its way inside the other

parts.note: tripe is nonsense or rubbish
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Bursting into a heap of junk fifty-three times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fifty-three' looks like one number, but splits into fifty (L) and the definition 'three times'.
explanation.definitionFit: Triple means threefold, multiplied by three.

clue.text: Local model about to quote me in provocation

indicators.note: about means the first pieces go round the others

parts.note: a local is a pub, an inn
to cite is to quote
the Model T was an early Ford car

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood model is about to quote me when provoked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sets the quote and me inside the pub and the car. 'Local' is British slang for one's nearby pub; the Model T was Ford's famous early car.
explanation.definitionFit: Incitement is urging someone on to act, a provocation.

clue.text: Pretty little angers horribly precocious kids

parts.note: twee means quaintly or affectedly pretty

indicators.note: horribly signals that angers is rearranged

explanation.surface: Sweet little things whose tempers are dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horribly' rearranges the angers into NAGERS. 'Pretty little' reads as describing the kids but is the twee part.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweenagers are children between childhood and teens, often precocious in tastes.

clue.text: Inclination to conceal surrounding problems

indicators.note: surrounding means the first word goes round the second

parts.note: to conceal is to hide
ills are troubles or problems

explanation.surface: A tendency to cover up the troubles around you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclination' looks like a tendency of mind, but here it is a physical slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A slope of a hill is an incline, so inclination is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Not a straight line

parts.note: a geometric shape that curves round on itself rather than running straight; also the name of a London Underground route that once ran in a loop

explanation.definitionFit: A closed curved figure is the obvious non-straight line, and the Circle line is a London Underground route.

clue.text: Classy wine with nothing for name causing raising of eyebrows

parts.note: U means upper class

indicators.note: nothing for name means O replaces N, nothing being O and name being N

parts.note: plonk is cheap wine

explanation.surface: Fancy wine replaced with nothing causes disapproving looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with nothing for name' swaps N (name) for O (nothing) in PLONK, giving PLOOK. U is a British label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: An uplook is an upward glance, which is what raised eyebrows produce.

clue.text: Line came across with poor effect to Latin characters

parts.note: to come across someone is to meet them, past tense met

indicators.note: the words poor and Latin are put to new effect, rearranged into fresh characters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone encountered a poorly rendered set of Latin letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'effect to' rearranges the poor Latin into ROPOLITAN. 'Line' is the definition, the London Underground route, not a row of text.
explanation.definitionFit: The Metropolitan line is one of the routes of the London Underground, so it is a line.

clue.text: 19th century effects not applicable on line

indicators.note: on means the abbreviation is placed after the line's name, attached to its end

parts.note: the Victoria line is a London Underground line

explanation.surface: Old possessions declared irrelevant on the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sends the abbreviation second. 'line' is the Victoria line of the London Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoriana are objects from the Victorian era, effects being belongings.

clue.text: Heard to choose a choice object on line

indicators.note: heard means the phrase is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: choose is pick, a stays, and a dilly is an excellent thing

explanation.surface: Listening to someone choosing a special item.
explanation.walkthrough: Dilly is slang for an outstanding example. The Piccadilly line is a London Underground line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Piccadilly line is one of London's Underground routes.

clue.text: Rite of entry into home, which houses aunt and uncle from Spain

parts.note: into gives IN

indicators.note: houses means the home word holds the relatives inside it

parts.note: in means at home
tia is Spanish for aunt (the 'from Spain' covers both relatives)
tio is Spanish for uncle

explanation.surface: A ceremony for entering a house that shelters one's Spanish aunt and uncle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spanish words for aunt and uncle are tia and tio; 'from Spain' covers both. 'in' for at home is a standard crossword equation.
explanation.definitionFit: An initiation is a ceremony admitting someone to a group, a rite of entry.

clue.text: Worthless attempt to conceal evidence of smoking

indicators.note: to conceal means the attempt hides the smoking trace inside it

parts.note: a try is an attempt
ash is what smoking leaves behind

explanation.surface: A feeble effort to hide signs of having smoked.
explanation.definitionFit: Trashy means cheap and of poor quality, without worth.

clue.text: Face of fool?

definitions.meaning: a gullible person, someone easily fooled

explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang senses: face in informal speech and a dupe or sucker, easily taken in.

clue.text: Throne rocked by ships of the line

indicators.note: rocked means shaken up, so throne is rearranged

parts.note: RN, the Royal Navy, is the ships

explanation.surface: A royal seat shaken by battleships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ships of the line' looks like a naval phrase, but 'line' is the definition: the Northern is a London Underground line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Northern line is one of London's Underground routes.

clue.text: Movement of authentication

indicators.note: of signals that the answer is a part taken out of the next word

explanation.surface: A gesture used to verify something.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'authentication', near its end.
explanation.definitionFit: A tic is an involuntary twitch, a small repeated movement of the muscles.

clue.text: Sailor, musician and extractor of fruit

parts.note: jack is a traditional word for a sailor
a horner is one who plays the horn

explanation.surface: A list of three people: a seaman, a player and a fruit picker.
explanation.walkthrough: In the English nursery rhyme, Little Jack Horner put in his thumb and pulled out a plum from a Christmas pie.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme boy pulls a plum out of his pie, so he is an extractor of fruit.

clue.text: Unity of spirit in opera?

parts.note: unity is one
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the theme of harmony appears in an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Onegin is Tchaikovsky's opera, named for its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Onegin is the title character of Tchaikovsky's opera, so he is found in opera.

clue.text: Yorkshire customs adopted by those who are up

definitions.text: adopted by those who are up

parts.note: a Riding was one of the three historic divisions of Yorkshire
habits are customs or practices

explanation.surface: Northern traditions taken up by people who are awake early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'those who are up' are people mounted on horseback, and 'adopted' means put on; Yorkshire was divided into three Ridings.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding habits are the outfits worn by horse riders, those who are up in the saddle.

clue.text: Hot type of play?

definitions.meaning: a burning piece of wood or a mark burnt in with hot iron, and also a type or make

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a firebrand or burned mark, and the title of Ibsen's drama.

clue.text: Mule out of control in the present unusual time

indicators.note: in means the jumbled letters go inside the present word

parts.note: a boon is a gift or present

indicators.note: out of control means mule is jumbled

explanation.surface: A mule runs amok during a gift giving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of control' scrambles the mule into LUEM, and 'in' places that inside the present.
explanation.definitionFit: Once in a blue moon means very rarely, so the phrase names a rare occasion.

clue.text: See 24
Say it was entirely English and get docked

parts.note: entirely means all

indicators.note: docked means cut short, so the last letter of get goes

explanation.surface: Claiming something was wholly English and gets its tail cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' removes the T from GET, as a dog's tail is docked.
explanation.definitionFit: To allege is to state or claim something, usually without proof, so say fits.

clue.text: Line to bear king and queen within

indicators.note: within means the royal pair sit inside the bear

parts.note: Baloo is the bear in Kipling's Jungle Book
K is the chess abbreviation for king
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is a crossword queen

explanation.surface: A queue made to put up with royalty in its midst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to bear' looks like 'to tolerate'; the bear is Baloo. The Bakerloo is a London Underground line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bakerloo line is one of the London Underground's routes, so it is a line.

clue.text: Never mind who has a line taken from material energy

indicators.note: taken from means the line letter is removed

parts.note: nylon is a synthetic material
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Whoever has had a strand pulled from cloth carrying power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken from' removes the line's letter from the fabric, leaving NYON. 'line' here is not the Underground, despite the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying any person at all, never mind who, is the idiom; whoever it is doesn't matter.

clue.text: Refuse one moving from prison

parts.note: dung is animal waste, refuse

indicators.note: moving signals that the letters of one are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone declines to leave jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb but is the noun, rubbish; ONE rearranged gives EON.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is an underground prison cell in a castle.
